concepts.name: Bengal Sultanate Architecture: Distinctive Features and Influences
key_dimensions: Use of locally available materials like brick and terracotta instead of stone, and its structural implications
Curvilinear roof (do-chala and char-chala) borrowed from Bengali vernacular huts — later influencing Mughal architecture
Eklakhi Mausoleum and Adina Mosque as benchmark examples — syncretic Hindu-Muslim elements
Contrast with Delhi Sultanate architecture: why Bengal evolved independently (geographic isolation, local patronage)

concepts.name: Jaunpur Sultanate (Sharqi) Architecture: The Propylon Gateway Style
key_dimensions: Massive sloping pylons (propylon-style) as a defining feature — distinguishing it from all other regional styles
Atala Mosque, Lal Darwaza Mosque, and Jami Masjid as canonical examples — structural analysis
Absence of minarets as a deliberate stylistic choice vs. other regional styles that retained them
UPSC trap: Jaunpur style is often confused with Tughlaq austerity — key differentiators

concepts.name: Malwa Sultanate Architecture: Afghan and Local Synthesis
key_dimensions: Use of dark red sandstone and marble — contrast with Bengal's brick and Jaunpur's stone
Hindola Mahal (swinging palace): unique battered/sloping side walls and their structural purpose
Jahaz Mahal at Mandu — caravanserai or harem debate, and its ship-like plan on a water body
Mandu as an integrated planned city: Baz Bahadur's palace and Rani Roopmati's pavilion — cultural context

concepts.name: Bahmani Sultanate Architecture: Persian Influence in the Deccan
key_dimensions: Strong Persian (Iranian) influence via imported architects — bulbous domes, pointed arches, tile-work (Kashan tiles)
Gulbarga Jami Masjid — anomaly: entire courtyard covered with a roof, unlike any other Indian mosque
Transition from Gulbarga to Bidar as capital and corresponding architectural evolution
UPSC trap: Distinguishing Bahmani from its successor Deccan Sultanate styles (Bijapur, Golconda)

concepts.name: Bijapur (Adil Shahi) Architecture: Gol Gumbaz and the Dome Tradition
key_dimensions: Gol Gumbaz — largest dome in India, second largest masonry dome in the world: pendentive squinch system
Ibrahim Rauza — considered more elegant than Taj Mahal by some historians: comparison of aesthetic principles
Whispering gallery phenomenon in Gol Gumbaz — acoustic architecture
UPSC trap: Gol Gumbaz vs. Taj Mahal dome construction technique — double dome vs. single dome distinction

concepts.name: Vijayanagara Architecture: Dravidian Revival with New Elements
key_dimensions: Continuation and elaboration of Dravidian style — massive gopurams, mandapas, and pillared halls (kalyana mandapa)
Introduction of new elements: horse and yali pillars, amman shrines, and enclosure walls
Hampi complex — Vittala Temple's stone chariot and musical pillars as engineering achievements
UPSC trap: Vijayanagara is NOT purely Dravidian — it incorporated Islamic and Chalukyan elements (syncretic nature)

concepts.name: Gujarat Sultanate Architecture: Hindu-Jain Craftsmen in Islamic Spaces
key_dimensions: Extensive use of Hindu and Jain craftsmen — resulting in intricate stone jali screens, corbelled arches, and torana motifs in mosques
Jami Masjid of Ahmedabad — 260 pillars, no minarets (broken by earthquake), exquisite stone tracery
Teen Darwaza and Sidi Saiyyed Mosque's jali as zenith of Indo-Islamic craftsmanship
UPSC trap: Gujarat style is often called 'Indo-Saracenic' loosely — distinguish from the 19th-century British Indo-Saracenic revival

concepts.name: Rajput Architecture: Fort-Palace Complexes and Defensive Urbanism
key_dimensions: Integration of fort, palace, temple, and water systems into a single complex — Chittorgarh, Amber, Mehrangarh
Jharokha (projecting balcony), chhatri (cenotaph pavilion), and shikhar towers as defining Rajput elements
Transition from purely defensive (Chittorgarh) to ceremonial-residential (City Palace, Udaipur) complexes
Influence on Mughal architecture — Akbar's adoption of Rajput jharokha and red sandstone at Fatehpur Sikri

concepts.name: Fatehpur Sikri: Synthesis of Regional Styles under Akbar
key_dimensions: Deliberate fusion of Gujarati, Rajput, and Persian elements — political symbolism of architectural synthesis
Panch Mahal: Buddhist-vihara-inspired stepped structure — anomaly in Mughal architecture
Buland Darwaza: built to commemorate Gujarat victory — highest gateway in India, its proportional features
UPSC trap: Fatehpur Sikri is largely red sandstone with limited marble — contrast with Shah Jahan's predominant marble use

concepts.name: Kerala Architecture: Nalukettu and Temple Architecture Traditions
key_dimensions: Thachu Shastra (traditional Kerala architecture treatise) — sloping tiled roofs adapted to high rainfall, distinct from pan-Indian norms
Nalukettu (four-sided courtyard house) as the template for both domestic and temple architecture
Padmanabhapuram Palace — largest wooden palace complex in Asia: structural and artistic features
UPSC trap: Kerala temples use circular (gajaprishtha) and rectangular shrines — NOT gopuram-dominated like Tamil Nadu

concepts.name: Kashmiri Architecture: Persian-Central Asian Synthesis in a Mountain Context
key_dimensions: Shah Hamadan Mosque (Khanqah-e-Moula) — distinctive pyramidal wooden roof with papier-mâché interiors: unique in Indian subcontinent
Use of deodar wood, lime mortar, and brick — adaptation to seismic and cold conditions
Martand Sun Temple ruins — pre-Islamic Kashmiri architecture showing Gandharan and classical Indian fusion
UPSC trap: Kashmiri Islamic architecture looks more Central Asian than South Asian — key differentiator from Mughal provincial styles

concepts.name: Odisha Temple Architecture: Nagara Sub-Style (Kalinga Order)
key_dimensions: Three distinct components: Rekha Deula (shikhara), Jagamohana (assembly hall), Natamandira (dance hall), Bhoga Mandapa
Konark Sun Temple — pancha ratha plan, erotic sculptures as spiritual symbolism (kama as a stage toward moksha)
UPSC trap: Kalinga style is a sub-type of Nagara — NOT Dravidian, though geographically in eastern India
Deula vs. Pidha distinction — different roof forms for different mandapa types within the same complex

concepts.name: Deccan Sultanate Comparative Architecture: Golconda, Ahmadnagar, and Bidar
key_dimensions: Golconda Fort's acoustic system — clap at the gateway audible at the summit: deliberate military engineering
Bidar's Persian tile-work and Bidriware craftsmanship linking architecture to decorative arts
Charminar, Hyderabad — four minarets marking intersection of trade routes: civic and religious symbolism combined
UPSC trap: Charminar is Qutb Shahi (Golconda Sultanate), NOT Bahmani or Mughal — common misattribution

concepts.name: Ahom Architecture: Brick Temples of Assam
key_dimensions: Unique shikhara form — hemispherical/beehive-shaped (not curvilinear Nagara or pyramidal Dravidian): distinct Eastern style
Kamakhya Temple and Umananda Temple — reconstruction history under Ahom rulers post-Muslim destruction
Use of locally fired bricks and lime-surkhi mortar — adaptation to Brahmaputra floodplain geology
UPSC trap: Ahom temples were built by a Tai-Shan dynasty that became Hinduized — cultural syncretism in architectural patronage

concepts.name: Colonial and Indo-Saracenic Architecture: British Synthesis of Indian Styles
key_dimensions: Indo-Saracenic Revival (19th–20th century) — British architects (Chisholm, Emerson, Stevens) combining Mughal, Rajput, and Gothic elements for colonial legitimacy
Chhatrapati Shivaji Maharaj Terminus (Victoria Terminus) — Gothic Revival with Indian decorative motifs: UNESCO World Heritage Site
Madras High Court and Mysore Palace — regional variation within Indo-Saracenic based on local patronage
UPSC trap: Indo-Saracenic is a BRITISH colonial invention — do NOT confuse with genuine medieval Indo-Islamic synthesis

concepts.name: Lutyens' Delhi: Imperial Classicism and its Indian Inflections
key_dimensions: Rashtrapati Bhavan — fusion of classical Baroque with Buddhist (Sanchi stupa dome) and Mughal (chhatris) elements
Deliberate symbolic choices: Jaipur Column, elephants on gates — imperial power encoded in architectural vocabulary
Herbert Baker's Secretariat Buildings vs. Lutyens' vision — the 'Bakerloo' controversy over gradient blocking Bhavan view
UPSC trap: Rashtrapati Bhavan dome is inspired by the Pantheon (Rome) AND Sanchi — dual heritage, often asked selectively

concepts.name: Chandigarh: Le Corbusier and the Post-Independence Modernist Experiment
key_dimensions: Capitol Complex (Secretariat, High Court, Assembly) — brutalist exposed concrete, brise-soleil sun-breakers adapted to Indian climate
Open Hand Monument — Le Corbusier's symbol of 'open to give, open to receive': ideological and aesthetic significance
UNESCO inscription (2016) as part of transnational Le Corbusier serial nomination — India's first modernist UNESCO site
UPSC trap: Chandigarh was designed after Nehru's invitation post-partition to build a new Punjab capital — political context essential

concepts.name: Rock-Cut Architecture: Continuity from Ancient to Medieval Regional Traditions
key_dimensions: Ellora Caves — three religious traditions (Buddhist, Hindu, Jain) in chronological sequence: Kailasa Temple (Cave 16) as monolithic achievement
Elephanta Caves — Rashtrakuta patronage, Trimurti as theological-architectural synthesis: UNESCO site
UPSC trap: Ajanta is Buddhist only; Ellora is multi-religious — a frequently tested distinction
Transition from rock-cut to structural temples — Pallava Mahabalipuram as the bridge (rathas = rock-cut; Shore Temple = structural)

concepts.name: Sikh Architecture: The Gurdwara Tradition and Harmandir Sahib
key_dimensions: Golden Temple (Harmandir Sahib) — four entrances symbolizing openness to all four directions/castes: ideological architecture
Fusion of Islamic (chhatris, pietra dura inlay) and Hindu (bangla roof, lotus motif) elements — deliberate Sikh syncretic identity
Akal Takht — temporal authority adjacent to spiritual authority: unique spatial theology
UPSC trap: The marble and gold embellishment was done by Maharaja Ranjit Singh in 19th century — original 16th-century structure was different

concepts.name: Maratha Architecture: Forts and Peshwa-era Wadas
key_dimensions: Hill forts (Raigad, Shivneri, Sinhagad) — strategic placement, self-sufficient water systems, and bastioned walls: military architecture
Shaniwar Wada, Pune — Peshwa residential complex blending Rajput and Mughal elements with Maratha pragmatism
UNESCO Maratha Military Landscapes (2024 nomination) — serial transboundary nomination context
UPSC trap: Maratha forts are NOT purely indigenous — they show Portuguese coastal fort influence (sea forts like Sindhudurg)
